The initial compass/current, magnet/coil and ring/log pairings were obvious in a pleasant way. Preserving quiet readings and distinguishing change from mere magnetic presence made me want the generator payoff; the final mechanical-energy explanation felt earned. I stalled after making the change argument because I had overlooked compass plus bar magnet. Hints on the argument, wire comparison and generator all had no partners, which briefly felt like a dead end; a compass hint restored momentum, and the direction-map branch then made sense. Communications was less engaging mechanically: I tried adding redundancy to the encoded message before sending it, and tried applying correction to the corrupted transmission, but both were rejected. The accepted order felt like arranging teaching labels rather than actually protecting and repairing a message. The explicit prefix-code example and 1.5-versus-2-bit calculation were the strongest reward there. Familiar direct combinations were often satisfying, but repeated abstract combinations and repeated cautions started to feel routine. I am stopping because these two resolved exhibits are a satisfying session and the next replication title does not make me eager to start another chain, not because I am blocked or required to stop. Four hints, seven rejected drops, no undo or revisits in my fresh play. This is my logical-interface experience, not a claim about human players or visual/touch usability.
